title: The CLI in CI/CD
summary: Inject vault secrets into any process with env pull, push, and run, using ONECLAW_TOKEN and ONECLAW_VAULT_ID in CI.

blocks.text: In a pipeline you don't want secrets committed to a repo or pasted into CI settings one by one. The CLI pulls them from a vault at runtime and injects them into your process.
In CI, authenticate with env vars instead of 1claw login: set ONECLAW_TOKEN (a JWT) or ONECLAW_API_KEY, plus ONECLAW_VAULT_ID for the vault to read.

steps.text: Set the non-interactive credentials in your shell or CI secrets store. Exchange your 1ck_ key at POST /v1/auth/api-key-token (see Foundations), or use your 1ck_ key directly as ONECLAW_API_KEY. Use the vault UUID from `1claw vault list` or from the Foundations track.
Seed your vault with a local .env file first.
Pull secrets into a .env file for tooling that reads one.
Or skip the file entirely and run a command with secrets injected as env vars. This is the safest option since nothing lands on disk.

blocks.text: CLI env commands (env push, env pull, env run) require @1claw/cli v0.38+. If you see errors on v0.37.x, use the API directly: curl -X PUT https://api.1claw.co/v1/vaults/$ONECLAW_VAULT_ID/secrets/config/env -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"type":"env_bundle","value":"KEY=value\nKEY2=value2"}'

blocks.caption: GitHub Actions step that pulls secrets from the vault

blocks.text: For offline or flaky-network builds, run 1claw env cache to store secrets in a local AES-256-GCM encrypted file (default TTL 300s). env run uses a valid cache automatically; add --no-cache to bypass it.
Your build process now starts with secrets injected straight from the vault, with no plaintext secrets checked into the repo or pasted into CI config.

quiz.question: Which command runs a process with vault secrets injected as env vars and nothing written to disk?
quiz.explanation: 1claw env run -- <cmd> injects secrets into the process environment directly.

quiz.question: Which two env vars typically authenticate and scope the CLI in CI?
quiz.explanation: ONECLAW_TOKEN (or ONECLAW_API_KEY) authenticates and ONECLAW_VAULT_ID scopes vault commands.

quiz.question: What does 1claw env cache store secrets in?
quiz.explanation: env cache writes an AES-256-GCM encrypted local file for offline env run.

title: The TypeScript SDK
summary: Install @1claw/sdk, create a client, and fetch a secret using the {data, error} response envelope.

blocks.text: The SDK gives Node apps and agents typed, full-parity access to the API. Every call returns an envelope so you check for errors without try/catch everywhere.

Auth options when creating a client: a personal API key (apiKey: '1ck_...') for server-side work, agent credentials (agentId + apiKey: 'ocv_...') which the SDK exchanges for a JWT and refreshes automatically, or manual login.

steps.text: Install the SDK in a Node 20+ project.
Set your key and vault ID in the environment so they stay out of source. Use your vault UUID from `1claw vault list`.

Write a script that creates a client and fetches a secret. Check res.error before using res.data. Use a path that exists in your vault, such as `api-keys/openai` from Foundations. Create one with `1claw secret set` if needed. Save the code above as `fetch-secret.ts`.
Run it.

blocks.text: Every method returns { data, error, meta }. Typed error classes like AuthError (401), NotFoundError (404), and RateLimitError (429) are exported from @1claw/sdk if you prefer to switch on the type.
You have a running script that authenticates with the SDK and prints a fetched secret value. That's the foundation for any Node service or agent that needs vault access.

quiz.question: What shape does every SDK method return?
options: A Promise that throws on any non-200
quiz.explanation: The SDK returns a { data, error, meta } envelope on every call.

quiz.question: How do you construct a client for server-side work with a personal key?
quiz.explanation: Pass baseUrl and apiKey (the 1ck_ personal key) to createClient.

quiz.question: When you pass agentId + apiKey (ocv_) to createClient, what does the SDK handle for you?
options: Exchanging credentials for a JWT and refreshing it before expiry
quiz.explanation: With agent credentials the SDK exchanges them for a JWT and refreshes it automatically.

title: Versioning and Rotation
summary: Rotate secrets server-side or with a client-supplied value, list version history, and disable old versions.

blocks.text: Every write to a path creates a new version and keeps the old ones. You can rotate in two ways: PUT a new value yourself, or have the vault generate a random one server-side so the plaintext never touches your client.

items: Client-supplied: PUT a new value to the same path, creating a new version
Server-side: POST to secret-rotate, the vault generates and stores the value
List: GET secret-versions returns all versions newest first with is_disabled
Disable: a disabled version is kept for audit but reads return 410 Gone

steps.text: Set your credentials. Use your 1ck_ key directly as a Bearer token, or exchange it at POST /v1/auth/api-key-token for a JWT (see Foundations). CLI steps assume you completed `1claw login` from the Install the CLI lesson.
Create the secret you will rotate. Skip this if it already exists from Foundations.
Rotate with a client-supplied value by PUTting a new value to the same path. This creates a new version.
Or rotate server-side. The vault generates a random 32-char hex value and stores it as the next version. You never see or send the plaintext.
Or do the same from the CLI.
List versions to confirm a new one exists.
Disable an old version so any read of it returns 410 Gone. Pick the oldest non-disabled version number from the list output above and use it in place of `1`.

blocks.text: For AI agents, the MCP tools mirror this: rotate_generate creates a random value server-side, rotate_and_store persists a value the agent already regenerated, and list_versions shows history with [disabled] markers.

You've rotated a secret to a fresh version and listed its history. Consumers reading the latest version pick up the new value automatically, and old versions can be disabled without losing the audit trail.

quiz.question: What's the key benefit of server-side rotation over a client PUT?
options: The generated plaintext is never sent to or returned from the client
quiz.explanation: Server-side rotation generates the value in the vault, so the plaintext never touches the client.

quiz.question: What does a read of a disabled version return?
quiz.explanation: Disabled versions are kept for audit but reads return 410 Gone.

quiz.question: Which MCP tool stores a value an agent already regenerated?
quiz.explanation: rotate_and_store persists a new value the agent supplies; rotate_generate makes one server-side.

title: Environment variables and bundles
summary: Use first-class per-key env vars with production/preview/development scoping, and know when the older env_bundle secret still fits.

blocks.text: Since v0.51, 1Claw stores environment variables as first-class per-key entries on a vault, with Vercel-style environment scoping. Each entry targets a specific environment — production, preview, development, or a custom one you define — and is encrypted individually. This replaced the older pattern of stuffing everything into a single env_bundle secret.

items: Vault-level vars live in the vault's env_vars store, addressed by KEY plus environment.
Org-level shared vars can be linked to many vaults at once, so a value like SENTRY_DSN is defined once.
Branch overrides let a preview deployment on feat/checkout get a different value than other previews.
Precedence is three-tier and always resolves in the same order: shared < vault < branch override.
Sensitive write-only mode makes a value non-readable after creation, even for humans.

blocks.text: Vault-level vars with the same KEY and environment always beat org-level shared vars. That is the whole conflict rule — there is no priority field to reason about.

steps.text: Create a vault-scoped variable for production.
Add a different value for preview, so preview deploys never touch the production database.
Resolve the final KEY=VALUE set for an environment. This is what a deploy or a runtime actually consumes.
Resolve with a branch override applied. If a branch-scoped value exists for feat/checkout it wins; otherwise you get the plain preview value.
Do the same from the CLI, which is what you would use in a deploy script.
steps.code:
1claw env ls
1claw env add DATABASE_URL "postgres://prod-host/app" -e production
1claw env environments ls

blocks.text: An agent connected over MCP calls the resolve_env tool to get the same resolved set, subject to its policies. It never sees values from an environment it is not scoped to.

The older approach — one env_bundle secret holding many KEY=VALUE lines — still works and still has a place. Use it when you want the whole set to move as a single versioned, rotatable unit, or when a consumer only knows how to read one secret. Reach for per-key env vars whenever you need environment scoping, shared org values, or branch overrides.

blocks.code:
# Legacy / single-unit pattern, still supported
1claw secret put app/env --type env --file .env
1claw env run -- node server.js
blocks.caption: The env_bundle pattern: one secret, one version, injected as a process environment

blocks.text: Cloud Runtimes merge resolved env vars into the container environment at start and rebuild. The combined set is capped at 64KB and a change needs a restart to take effect.

quiz.question: A vault defines DATABASE_URL for production, and an org-level shared var also defines DATABASE_URL for production. Which value wins?
options: The request fails with a conflict error
quiz.explanation: Precedence is shared < vault < branch override. A vault-level var with the same key and environment always beats the org-level shared var.

quiz.question: What does the git_branch query parameter add to an env-vars resolve call?
options: It applies a branch override on top of the environment's values
It creates a new environment named after the branch
It filters results to vars created on that branch
It is only used for audit logging
quiz.explanation: Branch overrides are the top tier of precedence, letting one feature-branch preview differ from other previews without defining a whole new environment.

quiz.question: When is the older env_bundle secret still the better fit?
options: When you want the whole set to version and rotate as one unit
When you need org-level shared values
It is deprecated and should never be used
quiz.explanation: env_bundle is not deprecated. It is the right tool when the set should move as a single versioned unit, or when the consumer can only read one secret. Per-key env vars are the choice when you need scoping, sharing, or branch overrides.

concepts.note: scoping by environment is an ABAC condition

title: Agent environment tagging
summary: Tag an agent as production or preview so its token, its policies, and its env var resolution all agree.

blocks.text: An agent can carry a named environment tag — production, preview, development, or a custom one. The tag is not a label for humans to read. It flows into the agent's JWT as an environment claim, it can gate policies, and it can drive env var resolution automatically.

items: environment_locked — once set at bootstrap it cannot be changed, so a production agent cannot be quietly relabelled.
env_auto_resolve — the resolve endpoint fills in the environment from the agent's tag instead of trusting a query parameter.
per_environment_guardrails — JSON overrides so the same agent definition enforces tighter limits in production.

blocks.text: Requires: an agent you can update, and a vault with env vars from the previous lesson.

steps.text: Create an agent tagged for production, locked so the tag cannot drift.
Confirm the tag landed. The JWT the agent exchanges for will now carry an environment claim.
Scope a policy to environments with the environment_in condition. This policy only grants access when the calling principal is tagged production.
Resolve env vars as the agent. Because env_auto_resolve is on, you omit the environment parameter entirely — the server uses the agent's tag.

blocks.text: Turn on the org setting env.enforce_agent_environment_scope to block agents from resolving variables outside their tagged environment. Without it, a preview-tagged agent can still ask for production values if a policy allows it.
The payoff is that one mistake stops being possible: a preview agent cannot read production values, because the environment is fixed in its identity rather than supplied per request.

quiz.question: Why does env_auto_resolve improve safety over passing ?environment=production?
options: The environment comes from the agent's identity instead of a caller-supplied parameter
It encrypts the resolved values in transit
It caches the resolved values for faster reads
It allows the agent to read every environment at once
quiz.explanation: A query parameter is supplied by the caller and can be changed. With env_auto_resolve the server reads the environment from the agent's own tag, so the agent cannot ask for a different one.

quiz.question: What does environment_locked prevent?
options: Changing the agent's environment tag after bootstrap
The agent reading any environment variables
quiz.explanation: environment_locked makes the tag immutable after bootstrap, so a production-scoped identity cannot later be relabelled as development to widen its access.

quiz.question: Which org setting stops a preview-tagged agent from resolving production variables?
quiz.explanation: env.enforce_agent_environment_scope blocks resolution outside the agent's tag. env.require_sensitive_prod is a different setting that forces prod and preview vars to be write-only.
